title: First Day at Work
summary: Dilnoza has just got her first job at a busy hotel. Everything goes wrong on her first morning, but she learns something important.
paragraphs: Dilnoza's alarm rang at five thirty, but she was already awake. Today was her first day as a receptionist at the Grand Hotel, the biggest hotel in the city. She had studied tourism for three years, and this was the job she had always wanted.

She put on the dark suit she had bought the week before, checked her hair three times and left the house early. But at the bus stop, she waited and waited. After twenty minutes, an old woman told her that the buses were not running because of road works. Dilnoza had to walk. She arrived at the hotel ten minutes late, out of breath, with her shoes hurting her feet.
The manager, Mr Rustamov, was waiting at the front desk. He did not look happy. “We start at seven here,” he said. “Not seven ten.” Dilnoza apologised and felt her face go red.

Her trainer was an experienced receptionist called Malika. She showed Dilnoza how to use the computer system to check guests in and out. It looked simple when Malika did it, but when Dilnoza tried, she pressed the wrong button and accidentally cancelled a booking. Malika fixed it quickly, but Dilnoza felt terrible.

At ten o'clock, a large group of tourists from Japan arrived. Malika was on the phone, so Dilnoza had to help them alone. She was nervous, but she remembered what she had learned in her studies. She smiled, spoke slowly and clearly, and checked each guest in carefully. One of the tourists did not speak English well, so Dilnoza used a translation app on her phone to explain where breakfast was served. The man bowed and thanked her.

Later that afternoon, an angry guest came to the desk. His room was too noisy, and he wanted his money back. Dilnoza listened patiently without interrupting. Then she apologised and found him a quiet room on the top floor. She also offered him a free breakfast. When he left, he was smiling.

At the end of the day, Mr Rustamov called Dilnoza into his office. She was sure he was going to talk about her being late. Instead, he said, “I saw how you helped the tour group and the guest with the noisy room. You stayed calm and kind. That is the most important skill in this job. The computer system you can learn. Being kind cannot be taught.”
Dilnoza walked home that evening with sore feet but a light heart. Tomorrow, she decided, she would leave the house even earlier.

questions.question: Why was Dilnoza late on her first day?
options: The buses were not running, so she walked
She went to the wrong hotel
questions.explanation: The buses were not running because of road works, so she had to walk.

questions.question: What mistake did Dilnoza make with the computer?
options: She cancelled a booking by accident
questions.explanation: She pressed the wrong button and accidentally cancelled a booking.

questions.question: How did Dilnoza help a tourist who did not speak English well?
questions.explanation: She used a translation app on her phone to explain where breakfast was served.

questions.question: What did Dilnoza do for the angry guest?
options: She gave all his money back
She found him a quiet room and offered free breakfast
questions.explanation: She found him a quiet room on the top floor and offered him a free breakfast.

questions.question: According to Mr Rustamov, what is the most important skill in the job?
questions.explanation: He said staying calm and kind is the most important skill.

grammar.explanation: Had + always + past participle describes something that was true for a long time before a past moment.
grammar.example: She had studied tourism for three years, and this was the job she had always wanted.

exercise.question: Choose the correct form: Before that day, Dilnoza ___ in a hotel.
exercise.explanation: We describe the time before a past moment, so we use had never worked.

grammar.structure: Passive with modal verbs (can be + past participle)
grammar.explanation: Can be / cannot be + past participle talks about what is possible or impossible to do to something.

exercise.question: Choose the correct sentence.
options: The problem can be fixed quickly.
The problem can be fix quickly.
The problem can being fixed quickly.
exercise.explanation: Modal passive: can be + past participle (fixed).
